title: Inclusion (Leviticus 19:14)
hook: no stumbling blocks: making community open to people with disabilities
tomorrow: show week, deadlines, no sleep. why won't Noa ask for help?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two teachers on one rule: the animal's own pain, or our practice of compassion. Animals feel. People, too, can be shut out without anyone meaning to.

A walker's rubber feet squeak across a synagogue floor, and stop. Ahead are the steps up to the bimah, the platform where the Torah is read, and the man with the walker has just been called up for an honor. Now what? He could quietly decline. Someone could haul him up. Or someone could ask why the steps are the only way. Leviticus has a line for this moment, in the JPS 1917 translation: "nor put a stumbling-block before the blind."
screen: `THE WALKER STOPS.` → `STEPS UP TO THE BIMAH.` → `"NOR PUT A STUMBLING-BLOCK."`

segments.voice: Read plainly, it's about a real obstacle in front of someone who can't see it. The rabbis also read it wider: don't trip up anyone who can't see the danger, like giving bad advice to someone who trusts you. In a community, both readings meet. A stumbling block isn't only a rock. It's steps with no ramp, a prayer book in type too small to read, a service with no way in for someone who is deaf, a room too loud for someone overwhelmed by noise. Then the verse goes on: "but thou shalt fear thy God." The commentator Rashi explains why: the person who was tripped can't know who did it, and only God sees. The commandment works where nobody is watching. And the Torah's own heroes needed things. Moses tells God he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. God doesn't replace him; Aaron is sent to speak with him. Leadership with an accommodation, inside the Torah itself. Lived, inclusion is removing one barrier at a time: a ramp, a large-print siddur, a quiet room, captions on the stream, or carrying the Torah down to someone who can't climb up to it.
screen: `ANY OBSTACLE THEY CAN'T SEE.` · `STEPS, SMALL TYPE, NOISE.` · `ONLY GOD SEES WHO SET IT.` · `MOSES, SLOW OF SPEECH.` · then, large: `NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.`

segments.voice: Stand, and walk slowly along the path from the nearest door to where you were sitting, as if your legs were tired or every sound were too loud. Feel each step, each edge, each thing in the way. Notice one barrier you'd never seen before, and whether it could be moved.
screen: `WALK THE PATH SLOWLY.` · `EACH STEP, EACH EDGE.` · `ONE BARRIER YOU NEVER SAW.`

segments.voice: Inclusion: a community with no stumbling blocks, where the way in works for every body and every mind.
One line for the road: no stumbling blocks, even the ones nobody else would notice. Eleven days of community and justice.

howItsDone: Many synagogues work on inclusion with ramps and accessible bimahs, large-print and braille prayer books, sign language or captions, and quiet spaces; some mark a Jewish disability awareness month each year.

what it means: remove any barrier, physical or not, from in front of someone who can't see it coming, especially where no one is watching.

chat.says: Mr. Feld got an aliyah, but the bimah has steps and he's on a walker. what do we do??
options: Remove the stumbling block: bring the reading to him, then push the shul for a ramp.
Let him decline the honor quietly. Some places just aren't built for everyone.
Have two guys carry him up fast so nobody notices the problem.
chat.meaning: Leviticus forbids putting a stumbling block before the blind, and the rabbis read it wide. Inclusion removes the barrier, not the person.
